name: media-card
description:
A card whose subject is a picture — an artifact thumbnail, a document preview, a generated image. The app has fifteen of these in a grid and the shape is doing something the plain `card` cannot: the media fills the card's whole upper area edge to edge, and the caption sits under it in a strip. A `card` pads its content; this one deliberately does not, because padding around a thumbnail wastes the only part of the card carrying information.

The placeholder is the part that gets skipped. A grid of these loads asynchronously, so most of them are empty most of the first second — and an empty card with no reserved height makes the whole grid reflow as each image lands.

base.$description:
A SQUARE tile with a 4px inset frame. Both halves of that were lost in the first extraction and both are the look: `ArtifactCard.svelte` is `aspect-square ... rounded-3xl border p-1`, and the padding is what makes the preview panel read as mounted inside a frame rather than bleeding to the card's edge. The extracted version had a 4:3 stage, `radius-md`, no padding, and a border under the caption doing the separating instead — four decisions, none of them the original's.

CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 100%` is the container's REQUIRED companion, not a preference. `container-type: inline-size` makes the box's width independent of its contents — that is the containment being asked for — so a container with no width of its own has nothing left to size from and collapses to zero. This unit did: centred in a grid it became a column of single words. A container fills what it is given and bounds itself with `max-inline-size`; it never sizes to its text.
base.transition: background var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out), border-color var(--duration-quick) var(--ease-out)

stage.$description: The preview, on its own WHITE ground rather than a tinted one — a scanned page or a photo has to be seen against paper, not against the card's cream. Its radius is the card's minus the 4px inset, which is what keeps the two curves concentric; matching them makes the inner panel look wrongly round.

caption.$description: No rule above it. The 4px frame already separates the caption from the preview, and adding a border draws a second line a few pixels from a real edge — which reads as a mistake rather than as structure.

kind.$description: Composes `badge badge--face-mono`. It was a bare colour on this unit while the original is a real pill on `surface-soft` — so the same file type read as a chip in the app and as grey text here.

meta.$description: Size and date, joined by a middot. It was missing entirely, which removed the only line on the tile that distinguishes two files with the same name — and the composition rule that a long list needs one differentiator.

placeholder.$description: What a file we cannot draw shows instead: its type, in mono, centred. Never an icon standing in for a preview — the type is the information.

ratio.$description: The tile's own shape. Square is the default because a grid of tiles is scanned, and a grid of differently-shaped tiles has no rhythm to scan.

page.$description: A document's proportions, for a shelf that is all paper.

selected.$description: A marine edge and the cream ground — the same pair the app uses, and not a tint alone: on a wall of tiles a fill change is easy to miss and the edge is what reads.

reducedMotion.$description: The lift goes; the border still warms.

a11y.note: ONE `<a>` around the whole card. The thumbnail is decorative — `alt=""` — because the title beside it is the name; an alt repeating the title makes a screen reader say it twice. Where the image IS the content and has no title, it takes a real alt instead. The kind chip is text, not colour: a file type conveyed only by a tint is a file type a colourblind user cannot read.
